content: The eradication of Helicobacter pylori using antimicrobial agents is recommended for patients with gastric or duodenal peptic ulcer disease who are colonized with H. pylori and for patients with mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. Additionally, eradication therapy should be considered for H. pylori-positive patients with immune thrombocytopenic purpura or those who have undergone resection for early-stage gastric cancer. The use of antibiotics in asymptomatic carriers is generally discouraged. Diagnostic Testing The American Journal of Gastroenterology guidelines recommend performing endoscopy to exclude peptic ulcer disease, esophagogastric malignancy, and other rare upper gastrointestinal tract diseases in the following scenarios: Dyspeptic patients over the age of 55 years, OR Dyspeptic patients with alarm features, such as: Gastrointestinal bleeding Anemia Early satiety Unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight Progressive dysphagia Odynophagia Persistent vomiting A family history of gastrointestinal cancer A history of esophagogastric malignancy Previously documented peptic ulcer, lymphadenopathy, or an abdominal mass For patients aged 55 years or younger without alarm features, two management strategies may be considered: 1. A test-and-treat approach using a validated non-invasive test (such as a urea breath test or stool antigen test) for H. pylori, followed by a trial of acid suppression if eradication is successful but symptoms persist. This is preferred in populations with a moderate to high prevalence of H. pylori infection (≥10%). 2. An empirical trial of acid suppression using a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) for 4–8 weeks, which is preferable in low-prevalence settings. Repeat endoscopy is not recommended once a definitive diagnosis of functional dyspepsia has been established, unless new symptoms or alarm features develop. Testing to confirm H. pylori eradication is most accurate when performed four weeks after completing therapy. Treatment Strategies The use of high-dose (twice daily) proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) enhances the efficacy of triple therapy. In regions with low clarithromycin resistance, clarithromycin-containing regimens (PCA or PCM) are recommended as first-line empirical treatments. Bismuth-containing quadruple therapy is also an alternative. In areas with high clarithromycin resistance, bismuth-containing quadruple therapy is the preferred first-line empirical treatment. If unavailable, sequential therapy is recommended. Extending the duration of triple therapy from 7 to 10–14 days improves eradication success rates and may be considered. After failure of a PPI-clarithromycin-containing therapy, either bismuth-containing quadruple therapy or levofloxacin-containing triple therapy (PLA) is recommended. After failure of second-line treatment, therapy should be guided by antimicrobial susceptibility testing whenever possible. Non-invasive tests, such as the urea breath test or a validated laboratory-based monoclonal stool test, are recommended to confirm the success of eradication therapy. Eradication Therapy for Helicobacter pylori Infection First-Line Therapies 1. Triple Therapy (PCA or PCM Regimen): Proton pump inhibitor (standard dose, twice daily) for 7–14 days Clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily) for 7–14 days Amoxicillin (1 g twice daily) for 7–14 days OR Metronidazole (250 mg four times daily) for 7–14 days 2. Quadruple Therapy: Proton pump inhibitor (standard dose, twice daily) for 10–14 days Metronidazole (250 mg four times daily) for 10–14 days Tetracycline (500 mg four times daily) for 10–14 days Bismuth (dose depends on preparation) for 10–14 days 3. Sequential Therapy: Proton pump inhibitor (standard dose, twice daily) for 5 days Amoxicillin (1 g twice daily) for 5 days Followed by: Proton pump inhibitor (standard dose, twice daily) for another 5 days Clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily) for another 5 days Tinidazole (500 mg twice daily) for another 5 days Second-Line Therapies 1. Triple Therapy (PLA Regimen): Proton pump inhibitor (standard dose, twice daily) for 10 days Levofloxacin (500 mg twice daily) for 10 days Amoxicillin (1 g twice daily) for 10 days 2. Triple Therapy (PMA Regimen): Proton pump inhibitor (standard dose, twice daily) for 7–14 days Metronidazole (250 mg four times daily) for 7–14 days Amoxicillin (1 g twice daily) for 7–14 days 3. Triple Therapy (PRA Regimen): Proton pump inhibitor (standard dose, twice daily) for 10 days Rifabutin (150–300 mg/day) for 10 days Amoxicillin (1 g twice daily) for 10 days Contraindicated Medications Bleeding peptic ulcer is considered an absolute contraindication to the use of the following medications: Ketorolac tromethamine Mefenamic acid Ticlopidine Prasugrel Reserpine Streptokinase Vorapaxar Guidelines and Resources American College of Gastroenterology (ACG): Guidelines for the management of dyspepsia.
